screens.title: Code Generation: Expressions and Statements
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we build the code generator: the compiler component that walks a parse tree and emits VM commands. You will learn why a symbol table is essential, how expressions become stack operations, and how each statement form maps to an idiomatic VM pattern. We use a stack-based VM model: expressions push values and apply operators, while statements use labels, jumps, and segment accesses. A concrete example you will revisit throughout is the expression x plus y times two, which demonstrates operator precedence and the need to follow the parse-tree structure. You will also see how method calls must push an implicit object reference so the called routine can access fields via the this segment. Along the way we will treat let, if, while, do, and return as fixed code templates the generator emits. By the end you should be able to read a parse tree, consult the symbol table for segment and index decisions, and produce VM sequences that the VM translator will execute. Think of the generator as a factory: the parse tree supplies parts, the symbol table supplies addresses, and the generator assembles VM output. What feels most challenging right now about emitting correct VM code?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will implement a code generator that translates parse trees into VM code and reason about why each VM instruction is emitted. First, you will learn to generate VM code for expressions: arithmetic, logical, and comparison operators. Converting an expression to code requires walking the parse tree and producing pushes and operator instructions in the correct order. Second, you will generate VM code for statements: let, if, while, do, and return. Each statement form maps to a clear VM template using segments, labels, and conditional jumps. Third, you will understand the symbol table structure: name, type, kind, and index for each identifier, and the difference between class-level and subroutine-level scoping. Finally, you will follow the visitor pattern to traverse a class and its subroutines, initializing symbol tables and emitting code for each statement. Each objective includes a small milestone so you can verify competency: emitting the correct sequence for a sample expression, producing templates for each statement, and resolving identifiers to the correct VM segment and index. Which milestone will you tackle first?

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice: building the generator incrementally and testing against reference VM outputs. Start by generating code for simple expressions and let statements. Then add if and while templates, and finally subroutine call conventions and constructors. Each step should be accompanied by a unit test that compares your VM output to the reference VM file. For expressions, test a variety of operator combinations and ensure the generated code respects precedence encoded in the parse tree. For statements, test both branches of the if-then-else pattern and loops that execute zero and multiple times. For subroutines, verify that method calls push the object reference first and that constructors invoke memory allocation. The milestone language focuses on measurable behavior: correct sequences for provided examples, correct segment/index selection, and successful invocation patterns. These practice milestones help you locate bugs by tracing the emitted VM code back to parse-tree nodes and symbol-table lookups.

screens.title: What the Code Generator Does
screens.narratorSegment: A code generator is the compiler backend that converts parse-tree nodes into VM instructions. Define it as a visitor: the generator traverses a class node, then visits each subroutine and statement node, emitting code as it goes. Practically this means the generator must initialize a subroutine-level symbol table for parameters and local variables, then walk statements and expressions to produce VM sequences. For example, when compiling a subroutine we define local variables in the symbol table, then iterate through each statement and call compile_statement on it. This pattern separates concerns: parsing produces a structured tree, the symbol table stores identifier metadata, and the generator focuses on producing correct VM operations based on those lookups. A common misconception is that the parse tree alone is sufficient to emit addresses; in practice the parse tree identifies names but does not carry allocation indices or segment decisions. The symbol table provides that mapping. A concrete example is compiling a method: before emitting the method body the generator defines parameter symbols, then uses their indices to emit push or pop instructions. Your takeaway: think of the generator as a disciplined walker that consults the symbol table every time it must emit an access or an argument.

keyIdea.title: Generator = Tree visitor
keyIdea.text: Traverse parse-tree nodes, consult symbol tables, and emit VM instructions accordingly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › What the Code Generator Does
Definition
A visitor that walks parse-tree nodes and emits VM commands, consulting the symbol table for addressing details.
def compile_subroutine(node):
  # init symbol table for params and locals
  for var_dec in node.var_decs:
    symbol_table.define(var_dec.name, var_dec.type, 'local')
  for statement in node.statements:
    compile_statement(statement)
Explanation
  • Visitor pattern provides a clear entry point per node type.
  • The symbol table is initialized per subroutine for locals and parameters.
  • Emitted VM code relies on symbol-table indices for segment selection.
Key Takeaway
Separation of concerns keeps parse trees small and symbol resolution centralized.

screens.title: Symbol Table Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: A symbol table stores metadata for each identifier: its name, type, kind, and index. Name and type are self-explanatory; kind tells you which VM segment to use — static, field, local, or parameter — and index is the offset within that segment. In practice the generator queries the symbol table when it needs to emit a push or pop. For example, compiling let x equals expression requires locating x's kind and index so the generator emits pop local i or pop field i, depending on the kind. Symbol tables are scoped: class-level tables hold static and field entries, while each subroutine gets a fresh table for parameters and locals. This avoids mixing scopes and makes lookup deterministic: when encountering an identifier the generator checks the subroutine table first, then the class table. A common misconception is to believe the parse tree provides enough information about where a variable lives. The parse tree names the variable, but it does not record indices or allocation decisions — that is the symbol table's job. A practical tip: maintain counters per kind to assign increasing indices as you define variables. This makes your generated segment indices stable and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Symbol table
keyIdea.text: Keeps name, type, kind, and index; scoped by class and subroutine to map identifiers to VM segments and offsets.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Symbol Table Essentials
Symbol Table Record
Each identifier stores four fields which guide code generation.
Name
The identifier string used in lookups.
Type
Primitive or class name used for size and semantic checks.
Kind
One of static, field, local, or parameter — selects VM segment.
Index
Offset within the chosen segment; assigned when defined.
Usage Patterns
  • Lookup yields kind and index for push/pop instructions.
  • Subroutine table is reinitialized for each subroutine.
  • Class table persists for static and field entries across subroutines.
Common Mistake
Assigning indices in multiple places leads to inconsistent addresses; centralize index counters per kind.

screens.title: Expression Code Generation
screens.narratorSegment: Expression generation follows a recursive pattern that matches the parse tree. The generator compiles each term so that its value is left on the VM stack, then applies operator instructions to combine values. Because the VM is stack-based, binary operations are implemented by first pushing operands, then issuing the operator command. Consider the example x plus y times two. The parser produces a tree where y times two is grouped as a subterm. The generator compiles the left term x by pushing its segment and index, then compiles the y times two subtree: it pushes y, pushes the constant two, emits multiply, and finally emits add. This order respects operator precedence encoded in parsing. A misconception is emitting operators in textual left-to-right order; instead, follow the parse tree's structure. For implementation, compile_expression often looks like: compile_term(first), then for each operator compile_term(next) and emit compile_operator(op). A concrete example mapped to VM code is: push local 0 for x, push local 1 for y, push constant 2, mult, add. Your job is to ensure that every compile_term leaves exactly one value on the stack and compile_operator consumes the top two values and pushes a result. How will you test that your expression generator respects precedence across mixed operators?

keyIdea.title: Expressions → stack ops
keyIdea.text: Compile terms recursively so each operator applies to values on the stack in the order determined by the parse tree.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Expression Code Generation
Pattern
Each term leaves one value on the stack. Operators consume top values and push results.
// x + y * 2
push local 0    // x
push local 1    // y
push constant 2
mult
add
Checklist
  • Follow parse-tree grouping to respect precedence.
  • Ensure compile_term leaves exactly one stack value.
  • Emit correct VM opcode for each operator mapping.
Common Mistake
Emitting operator commands before pushing all operand values breaks stack ordering.

screens.title: Operator Precedence and Parse Trees
screens.narratorSegment: Operator precedence is enforced by the grammar and the parse tree, not by the code generator scanning tokens left to right. The generator's job is to mirror the tree: when a subtree groups higher-precedence operations, compile that subtree before composing results at the parent. For example, in x plus y times two the parse tree has a multiplication subtree for y times two. When compiling, the generator first compiles the multiplication subtree, which pushes y and 2 and emits multiply. It then compiles the remaining addition by pushing x and emitting add after the multiplication result is on the stack. If the generator instead naively emitted instructions in the textual sequence x, plus, y, times, two, the VM stack would receive operands and operators out of order, yielding incorrect results. An important test is to write expressions that mix addition, multiplication, and parentheses; when you see the same VM sequence as the reference, precedence is preserved. A misconception to watch for is treating operators as immediate commands rather than as actions on already-pushed operands. Your rubric: confirm that each operator's operands are on the stack immediately before the operator command appears.

keyIdea.title: Follow the tree
keyIdea.text: The parse tree encodes precedence; the generator must compile subtrees in the order the tree prescribes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Operator Precedence
Why precedence matters
Precedence determines grouping in the parse tree, which in turn determines the order of pushes and operator emissions.
1. The parser groups higher-precedence operators into subtrees.
2. The generator compiles each subtree to leave a value on the stack.
3. Parent nodes combine values with operator commands.
Quick test
Construct expressions mixing addition and multiplication and compare your VM output to the reference to confirm correct ordering.
Takeaway
Always compile by tree structure; never by raw token order.

screens.title: Let Statement Template
screens.narratorSegment: A let statement assigns the result of an expression to a variable. The generator first emits code to evaluate the expression, leaving its value on the stack. Then it emits a pop instruction to store that value in the correct segment and index determined by the symbol table. For example, let x equals expression becomes: generate code for expression so the result sits on the stack, then pop local i where i is x's index in the local segment. This split — compute then store — simplifies correctness: you only need to guarantee expression evaluation semantics, and variable assignment becomes a single pop. A common pitfall is popping before the expression is fully evaluated or using the wrong segment because of incorrect kind resolution. To avoid this, always consult the symbol table immediately before emitting the pop. A concrete scenario: compiling let arr 2 equals x plus 3 requires computing x plus 3, pushing the index for arr plus offset, and then using pop to store. The takeaway: assignment maps to a fixed two-step VM pattern that relies on accurate symbol-table lookup.

keyIdea.title: Let rule
keyIdea.text: Evaluate the right-hand expression, then pop the result to the segment/index provided by the symbol table.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Let Statement Template
Pattern
Compute expression → pop to variable's segment/index.
// let x = expression;
// generate code for expression
pop local i   // i is index of x in symbol table
Notes & Example
Before pop, confirm the symbol table kind: static, field, local, or parameter. Using wrong segment leads to runtime errors or wrong data reads.
Pro Tip
Always query symbol_table.kind and symbol_table.index once just before emitting the pop to avoid stale state.

screens.title: If-Then-Else VM Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The if statement compiles to a predictable VM sequence using labels and conditional jumps. The generator evaluates the condition expression to leave a boolean value on the stack. It then emits an if-goto instruction to jump to the else label when the condition is false. The true-branch code follows, then an unconditional goto to skip the else branch. Labels mark the else and end locations. A typical emitted pattern is: generate condition, if-goto ELSE, compile statements1, goto END, label ELSE, compile statements2, label END. One common misconception is reversing the jump sense — remember that if-goto jumps when the top of stack is true, so structure the labels accordingly. A concrete example: compiling if (x < y) { do A } else { do B } requires emitting the comparison code that leaves true if x is less than y, then if-goto ELSE, then code for A, then goto END, label ELSE, code for B, label END. Your test should include both branches executing and the case where the condition is false from the start. This pattern keeps branching explicit and easy to debug in VM output.

keyIdea.title: If template
keyIdea.text: Condition → if-goto ELSE → true-branch → goto END → label ELSE → false-branch → label END.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › If Statement Pattern
Pattern Example
// if (expression) { statements1 } else { statements2 }
// generate expression
if-goto ELSE
// statements1
goto END
label ELSE
// statements2
label END
Tips
  • Generate a fresh unique label for ELSE and END per if instance.
  • Remember if-goto jumps when the condition is true; invert logic accordingly.
  • Test both branches and edge cases where the condition is false immediately.
Common Mistake
Reusing labels across different ifs causes incorrect jumps; ensure uniqueness.

screens.title: While Loop Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A while loop compiles to a small control-flow pattern that repeats body code while a condition holds. The generator creates a LOOP label at the top, generates the condition so a boolean is pushed, emits if-goto to the body or to the END depending on your chosen sense, compiles the statements, emits an unconditional goto back to LOOP, and finally emits label END. The chapter gives a canonical sequence: label LOOP, generate expression, if-goto END, generate statements, goto LOOP, label END. Careful label placement matters: the condition must be evaluated before deciding to execute the body. One misconception is emitting goto LOOP before the body, which can produce an infinite loop if the condition is not checked first. Test loops with zero iterations by compiling a condition that evaluates to false initially; the END label should be reached without executing the body. Implement unique labels per loop instance. The takeaway is that while loops are a small finite template that, when implemented consistently, yields predictable VM behavior and simplifies debugging. While Loop Pattern means label loop → evaluate condition → if-goto end → body → goto loop → label end.. In practical terms, label, condition, body, and loop back. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Canonical Sequence
// while (expression) { statements }
label LOOP
// generate expression
if-goto END
// generate statements
goto LOOP

  • Ensure the condition evaluation pushes a boolean before if-goto.
  • Test zero-iteration cases to confirm correct branching to END.

screens.title: Do and Return Statements
screens.narratorSegment: Do and return statements are small but important patterns. A do statement invokes a subroutine for its side effects and discards the return value. The generator emits code for the subroutine call and then pops the return value into temp 0 to drop it. For a return statement, the generator compiles the expression if any, leaving the result on the stack, and then emits the VM return command. If the subroutine returns void, the generator must still ensure the VM sees a value on the stack only if the VM return semantics require it; in the Jack VM the return instruction uses whatever is on the top of the stack as the return value. A common mistake is forgetting to discard a return value from a do call, which leaves stale data on the stack and corrupts subsequent operations. For example, compiling do Square. draw(); should produce the call sequence followed by pop temp 0. For return x + 1, generate the expression then emit return. These patterns are concise templates: call then pop for do, evaluate then return for return. Reflect: how will you ensure your calls uniformly handle returned and discarded values?

keyIdea.title: Do vs Return
keyIdea.text: Do: call then pop temp 0 to discard. Return: evaluate optional expression then issue return so VM receives the result.

content.html:

screens.title: Subroutine Call Conventions
screens.narratorSegment: Subroutine calls differ by kind and require specific argument arrangements. For a method call like obj. method(args), the generator must push the object reference as the first argument, then push explicit arguments, and then emit call. This implicit object reference becomes the called routine's this pointer. For a function call ClassName. function(args), there is no implicit this, so only explicit arguments are pushed before calling. Constructors require memory allocation: the generator pushes the number of fields, calls Memory. alloc to obtain space, and then pushes the returned object reference before calling the constructor to initialize fields. A concrete scenario: to call obj. set(5), emit push that object's segment and index to get its reference, push constant 5, then call obj. set with two arguments. A common error is forgetting to push the object for method calls which leaves the called routine without a valid this pointer. Another is forgetting to allocate memory for constructors leading to uninitialized this. The takeaway: follow the precise sequence per subroutine type so the callee receives the expected argument layout and this pointer. Subroutine Call Conventions means method: push object reference then args. function: push args. constructor: allocate object, push reference, then call initializer.. In practical terms, method vs function vs constructor in vm code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Visitor Structure
Pipeline
def compile_class(node):
  for subroutine in node.subroutines:
    compile_subroutine(subroutine)

def compile_subroutine(node):
  # init symbol table for parameters and locals
  for var_dec in node.var_decs:
    symbol_table.define(var_dec.name, var_dec.type, 'local')
  for statement in node.statements:
    compile_statement(statement)

def compile_expression(node):
  compile_term(node.terms[0])
  for i, op in enumerate(node.operators):
    compile_term(node.terms[i+1])
    compile_operator(op)
Test each function independently. For example, pass a small expression node to compile_expression and verify the VM sequence before testing statement-level templates.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debug Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing a generator, a few recurrent mistakes surface. First, incorrect symbol-table indices cause wrong segment accesses; you will see push local 0 when the reference should be field 2. Fix this by centralizing index assignment and inspecting the symbol-table state at subroutine entry. Second, operator order errors occur when code is emitted in token order rather than tree order, breaking precedence. Use small expression tests and compare VM sequences to references. Third, label reuse across ifs and loops produces jump collisions; generate unique labels per construct, often by incrementing a counter. Fourth, forgetting to push the object reference for method calls leaves the callee without a valid this. Ensure your method-call path always pushes the object reference before explicit args. Fifth, not discarding return values from do statements will leak values on the stack; add pop temp 0 after every do. For debugging, trace the emitted VM and map each instruction back to the parse-tree node and symbol-table lookup that produced it. The practical tip is to keep each compile_* routine small and testable so you can isolate the failing stage quickly. Which of these checks will you add to your unit-test suite first?

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we build the code generator: the compiler component that walks a parse tree and emits VM commands. You will learn why a symbol table is essential, how expressions become stack operations, and how each statement form maps to an idiomatic VM pattern. We use a stack-based VM model: expressions push values and apply operators, while statements use labels, jumps, and segment accesses. A concrete example you will revisit throughout is the expression x plus y times two, which demonstrates operator precedence and the need to follow the parse-tree structure. You will also see how method calls must push an implicit object reference so the called routine can access fields via the this segment. Along the way we will treat let, if, while, do, and return as fixed code templates the generator emits. By the end you should be able to read a parse tree, consult the symbol table for segment and index decisions, and produce VM sequences that the VM translator will execute. Think of the generator as a factory: the parse tree supplies parts, the symbol table supplies addresses, and the generator assembles VM output. What feels most challenging right now about emitting correct VM code?

By the end of this chapter you will implement a code generator that translates parse trees into VM code and reason about why each VM instruction is emitted. First, you will learn to generate VM code for expressions: arithmetic, logical, and comparison operators. Converting an expression to code requires walking the parse tree and producing pushes and operator instructions in the correct order. Second, you will generate VM code for statements: let, if, while, do, and return. Each statement form maps to a clear VM template using segments, labels, and conditional jumps. Third, you will understand the symbol table structure: name, type, kind, and index for each identifier, and the difference between class-level and subroutine-level scoping. Finally, you will follow the visitor pattern to traverse a class and its subroutines, initializing symbol tables and emitting code for each statement. Each objective includes a small milestone so you can verify competency: emitting the correct sequence for a sample expression, producing templates for each statement, and resolving identifiers to the correct VM segment and index. Which milestone will you tackle first?

This second objectives slide focuses on practice: building the generator incrementally and testing against reference VM outputs. Start by generating code for simple expressions and let statements. Then add if and while templates, and finally subroutine call conventions and constructors. Each step should be accompanied by a unit test that compares your VM output to the reference VM file. For expressions, test a variety of operator combinations and ensure the generated code respects precedence encoded in the parse tree. For statements, test both branches of the if-then-else pattern and loops that execute zero and multiple times. For subroutines, verify that method calls push the object reference first and that constructors invoke memory allocation. The milestone language focuses on measurable behavior: correct sequences for provided examples, correct segment/index selection, and successful invocation patterns. These practice milestones help you locate bugs by tracing the emitted VM code back to parse-tree nodes and symbol-table lookups.

A code generator is the compiler backend that converts parse-tree nodes into VM instructions. Define it as a visitor: the generator traverses a class node, then visits each subroutine and statement node, emitting code as it goes. Practically this means the generator must initialize a subroutine-level symbol table for parameters and local variables, then walk statements and expressions to produce VM sequences. For example, when compiling a subroutine we define local variables in the symbol table, then iterate through each statement and call compile_statement on it. This pattern separates concerns: parsing produces a structured tree, the symbol table stores identifier metadata, and the generator focuses on producing correct VM operations based on those lookups. A common misconception is that the parse tree alone is sufficient to emit addresses; in practice the parse tree identifies names but does not carry allocation indices or segment decisions. The symbol table provides that mapping. A concrete example is compiling a method: before emitting the method body the generator defines parameter symbols, then uses their indices to emit push or pop instructions. Your takeaway: think of the generator as a disciplined walker that consults the symbol table every time it must emit an access or an argument.

A symbol table stores metadata for each identifier: its name, type, kind, and index. Name and type are self-explanatory; kind tells you which VM segment to use — static, field, local, or parameter — and index is the offset within that segment. In practice the generator queries the symbol table when it needs to emit a push or pop. For example, compiling let x equals expression requires locating x's kind and index so the generator emits pop local i or pop field i, depending on the kind. Symbol tables are scoped: class-level tables hold static and field entries, while each subroutine gets a fresh table for parameters and locals. This avoids mixing scopes and makes lookup deterministic: when encountering an identifier the generator checks the subroutine table first, then the class table. A common misconception is to believe the parse tree provides enough information about where a variable lives. The parse tree names the variable, but it does not record indices or allocation decisions — that is the symbol table's job. A practical tip: maintain counters per kind to assign increasing indices as you define variables. This makes your generated segment indices stable and predictable.

Expression generation follows a recursive pattern that matches the parse tree. The generator compiles each term so that its value is left on the VM stack, then applies operator instructions to combine values. Because the VM is stack-based, binary operations are implemented by first pushing operands, then issuing the operator command. Consider the example x plus y times two. The parser produces a tree where y times two is grouped as a subterm. The generator compiles the left term x by pushing its segment and index, then compiles the y times two subtree: it pushes y, pushes the constant two, emits multiply, and finally emits add. This order respects operator precedence encoded in parsing. A misconception is emitting operators in textual left-to-right order; instead, follow the parse tree's structure. For implementation, compile_expression often looks like: compile_term(first), then for each operator compile_term(next) and emit compile_operator(op). A concrete example mapped to VM code is: push local 0 for x, push local 1 for y, push constant 2, mult, add. Your job is to ensure that every compile_term leaves exactly one value on the stack and compile_operator consumes the top two values and pushes a result. How will you test that your expression generator respects precedence across mixed operators?

Operator precedence is enforced by the grammar and the parse tree, not by the code generator scanning tokens left to right. The generator's job is to mirror the tree: when a subtree groups higher-precedence operations, compile that subtree before composing results at the parent. For example, in x plus y times two the parse tree has a multiplication subtree for y times two. When compiling, the generator first compiles the multiplication subtree, which pushes y and 2 and emits multiply. It then compiles the remaining addition by pushing x and emitting add after the multiplication result is on the stack. If the generator instead naively emitted instructions in the textual sequence x, plus, y, times, two, the VM stack would receive operands and operators out of order, yielding incorrect results. An important test is to write expressions that mix addition, multiplication, and parentheses; when you see the same VM sequence as the reference, precedence is preserved. A misconception to watch for is treating operators as immediate commands rather than as actions on already-pushed operands. Your rubric: confirm that each operator's operands are on the stack immediately before the operator command appears.

A let statement assigns the result of an expression to a variable. The generator first emits code to evaluate the expression, leaving its value on the stack. Then it emits a pop instruction to store that value in the correct segment and index determined by the symbol table. For example, let x equals expression becomes: generate code for expression so the result sits on the stack, then pop local i where i is x's index in the local segment. This split — compute then store — simplifies correctness: you only need to guarantee expression evaluation semantics, and variable assignment becomes a single pop. A common pitfall is popping before the expression is fully evaluated or using the wrong segment because of incorrect kind resolution. To avoid this, always consult the symbol table immediately before emitting the pop. A concrete scenario: compiling let arr 2 equals x plus 3 requires computing x plus 3, pushing the index for arr plus offset, and then using pop to store. The takeaway: assignment maps to a fixed two-step VM pattern that relies on accurate symbol-table lookup.

The if statement compiles to a predictable VM sequence using labels and conditional jumps. The generator evaluates the condition expression to leave a boolean value on the stack. It then emits an if-goto instruction to jump to the else label when the condition is false. The true-branch code follows, then an unconditional goto to skip the else branch. Labels mark the else and end locations. A typical emitted pattern is: generate condition, if-goto ELSE, compile statements1, goto END, label ELSE, compile statements2, label END. One common misconception is reversing the jump sense — remember that if-goto jumps when the top of stack is true, so structure the labels accordingly. A concrete example: compiling if (x < y) { do A } else { do B } requires emitting the comparison code that leaves true if x is less than y, then if-goto ELSE, then code for A, then goto END, label ELSE, code for B, label END. Your test should include both branches executing and the case where the condition is false from the start. This pattern keeps branching explicit and easy to debug in VM output.

A while loop compiles to a small control-flow pattern that repeats body code while a condition holds. The generator creates a LOOP label at the top, generates the condition so a boolean is pushed, emits if-goto to the body or to the END depending on your chosen sense, compiles the statements, emits an unconditional goto back to LOOP, and finally emits label END. The chapter gives a canonical sequence: label LOOP, generate expression, if-goto END, generate statements, goto LOOP, label END. Careful label placement matters: the condition must be evaluated before deciding to execute the body. One misconception is emitting goto LOOP before the body, which can produce an infinite loop if the condition is not checked first. Test loops with zero iterations by compiling a condition that evaluates to false initially; the END label should be reached without executing the body. Implement unique labels per loop instance. The takeaway is that while loops are a small finite template that, when implemented consistently, yields predictable VM behavior and simplifies debugging. Do and return statements are small but important patterns. A do statement invokes a subroutine for its side effects and discards the return value. The generator emits code for the subroutine call and then pops the return value into temp 0 to drop it. If the subroutine returns void, the generator must still ensure the VM sees a value on the stack only if the VM return semantics require it; in the Jack VM the return instruction uses whatever is on the top of the stack as the return value.
